summary.case_overview: This judgment arises from Writ Petition (Civil) 135 of 1970 filed under Article 32 of the Constitution by Kesavananda Bharati against the State of Kerala, challenging the constitutional validity of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1972, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972, the last of which placed the impugned Kerala land reform enactments into the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 2]. The petitioner was permitted to amend the petition to challenge these constitutional amendments [Page 1] [Page 2]. A 13-Judge Bench was constituted to determine the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, whether I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was correctly decided, whether there are inherent or implied limitations on the amending power, and the validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 104] [Page 129] [Page 142] [Page 194] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501] [Page 502].
summary.facts_of_case: On March 21, 1970, the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31, praying that the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964) as amended by the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 (Act 35 of 1969) be declared unconstitutional and void [Page 1]. The Supreme Court issued rule nisi on March 25, 1970 [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 (Kerala Act 25 of 1971) received Presidential assent on August 7, 1971 [Page 1]. Meanwhile, in Kunjukutty Sahib v. State of Kerala, the Supreme Court upheld the Kerala High Court judgment striking down certain sections of the land reform legislation [Page 1] [Page 2]. Parliament subsequently enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act on November 5, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act on April 20, 1972, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act on June 9, 1972, which placed Kerala Acts 35 of 1969 and 25 of 1971 into the Ninth Schedule [Page 2]. On August 10, 1972, the Court allowed the petitioner to amend the writ petition to challenge the validity of these constitutional amendments and referred the matter to a 13-Judge Bench [Page 1] [Page 2].
summary.legal_issues: The major legal issues discussed in the judgment are: (1) What is the source, nature, and extent of the amending power conferred on Parliament under Article 368 of the Constitution, and whether it is derived from Article 368 itself or from residuary legislative powers under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of List I [Page 2] [Page 309] [Page 501]; (2) Whether I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was correctly decided in holding that fundamental rights cannot be abridged or taken away by constitutional amendments and that a constitutional amendment is 'law' within Article 13(2) [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 117] [Page 484] [Page 501]; (3) Whether there are inherent or implied limitations on Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 preventing the abrogation or destruction of the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution [Page 6] [Page 91] [Page 104] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 487] [Page 501]; (4) Whether the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 is constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 494] [Page 501]; (5) Whether Section 2 and Section 3 (introducing Article 31C) of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1972 are constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 194] [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 374] [Page 495] [Page 498] [Page 501]; and (6) Whether the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 is constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 501].
summary.important_arguments_or_content:
Arguments by the Petitioners: Counsel for the petitioners contended that Parliament's power under Article 368 is limited and does not extend to destroying the basic structure, essential features, or identity of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 91] [Page 258] [Page 488]. They argued that fundamental rights are natural, inalienable, primordial rights based on universal human rights, which cannot be taken away or abridged by constitutional amendment [Page 181] [Page 487] [Page 488]. They submitted that the word 'amendment' in Article 368 has a narrow meaning distinct from repeal or abrogation [Page 78] [Page 232]. They further argued that Article 31C subverts essential features, delegates amending power to State Legislatures, and unlawfully excludes judicial review through its declaration clause [Page 245] [Page 496].

Arguments by the Respondents: Counsel for the respondents argued that Article 368 confers an unlimited constituent power on Parliament to amend any provision of the Constitution, short of total repeal [Page 2] [Page 91] [Page 104]. They contended that an amendment under Article 368 is made in exercise of constituent power, not ordinary legislative power, and is not 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) [Page 3] [Page 155] [Page 486]. They submitted that there are no inherent or implied limitations on the amending power, and that Parliament can abrogate fundamental rights to achieve Directive Principles and construct an egalitarian social order [Page 2] [Page 78] [Page 104] [Page 194] [Page 484] [Page 497].
summary.court_reasoning: The Court's reasoning across various opinions established the following major points: (1) Source of Power and Overruling Golak Nath: The Court held that the power to amend the Constitution is derived from Article 368 itself, not from residuary Entry 97 of List I or Articles 245/248, and that a constitutional amendment made under Article 368 in exercise of constituent power is not 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) [Page 3] [Page 129] [Page 155] [Page 309] [Page 486] [Page 501]. (2) Basic Structure and Amending Power: Sikri C.J., Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, and Jaganmohan Reddy JJ. reasoned that while Article 368 confers wide amending power, 'amendment' does not include the power to completely abrogate, emasculate, or destroy the basic structure or essential elements of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 104] [Page 129] [Page 258]. Ray, Palekar, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, and Chandrachud JJ. held that the power under Article 368 is wide, plenary, and unfettered, reaching every part of the Constitution without implied or inherent limitations [Page 155] [Page 181] [Page 271] [Page 296] [Page 425] [Page 484] [Page 488] [Page 501]. Khanna J. held that Article 368 confers power to amend all articles, including fundamental rights, but the word 'amendment' does not permit altering or abrogating the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 309] [Page 335] [Page 374]. (3) Validity of 24th Amendment: The Court held the 24th Amendment valid as declaring and clarifying that Parliament possesses constituent power to amend any provision under Article 368 and that Article 13(2) does not apply [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 494] [Page 501]. (4) Validity of 25th Amendment: Section 2 substituting 'amount' for 'compensation' in Article 31(2) was upheld, with the reasoning that while 'just equivalent' is no longer required, the amount fixed or principles determined must not be illusory or arbitrary [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 497] [Page 498] [Page 501]. For Section 3 (Article 31C), the first part protecting laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) from Articles 14, 19, and 31 was upheld subject to judicial review for direct and reasonable nexus [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 425] [Page 500] [Page 501]; however, the second part ('and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy') was held invalid and severed because it ousted judicial review and struck at the basic structure [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501] [Page 502]. (5) Validity of 29th Amendment: The 29th Amendment inserting Kerala Acts into the Ninth Schedule was held valid under Article 31B [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 501].

State of Punjab was overruled regarding the source of amending power and the application of Article 13(2) to constitutional amendments [Page 258] [Page 309] [Page 501]; (2) The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 is valid [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 494] [Page 501]; (3) Section 2(a) and Section 2(b) of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1972 are valid [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 498] [Page 501]; (4) Section 3 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1972 (introducing Article 31C) is valid except for the declaration clause ('and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy'), which was declared unconstitutional and severed [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501] [Page 502]; (5) The Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 is valid [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501]; and (6) The cases and writ petitions were remitted to the Constitution Bench for determination in accordance with law [Page 374] [Page 502].

summary.simplified_explanation: In this major case, a 13-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court examined whether Parliament has unlimited power to change the Indian Constitution [Page 1] [Page 2]. The Court decided that Parliament does have the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, and reversed its earlier Golak Nath judgment which restricted amendments [Page 129] [Page 309] [Page 501]. However, the Court ruled that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is not unlimited: Parliament cannot alter, destroy, or abrogate the 'basic structure' or essential framework of the Constitution [Page 104] [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 374]. The Court upheld the 24th Amendment (confirming Parliament's constituent power to amend) and the 29th Amendment (protecting state land reform laws) [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501]. Regarding the 25th Amendment, the Court allowed replacing 'compensation' with 'amount' for land acquisitions so long as the amount is not fake or arbitrary [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 498] [Page 501]. For Article 31C, the Court allowed protecting laws that carry out specific socio-economic Directive Principles (Article 39(b) and (c)) from fundamental rights challenges, but struck down the portion that attempted to stop courts from checking whether a law actually served those principles [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501] [Page 502].
